name: Italian Game
personality: The classic: quick development, aim at f7, castle early. Calm or sharp, your choice.
story: One of the oldest openings in chess. Italian masters of the 1500s–1600s, like Gioachino Greco, wrote about it. Its slow main line is called the Giuoco Piano, Italian for "quiet game".
famous: Still a favourite of world champions today, from Carlsen to Ding Liren.
fact: Greco's 1620s games with the Italian include some of the oldest recorded traps still taught today.
memory: Bishop to c4 points straight at f7 — Black's weakest square, guarded only by the king.
when: Great as a first opening and for any style. Play c3 + d3 for slow manoeuvring, or d4 for open fights.
ideas: Develop knights and bishops fast, then castle.
Play c3 and d3 (or d4) to build a strong centre.
The bishop on c4 (later b3) keeps pressure on f7 all game.
Re1, Nbd2–f1–g3 is a typical knight route to the kingside.
watch: After 3...Nf6 you can try 4.Ng5 (attacking f7), but Black answers 4...d5! and it gets sharp.
Don't grab pawns early with your queen — Black develops with tempo.

name: Ruy López
personality: The Spanish torture: slow, deep pressure on Black's centre for the whole game.
story: Named after Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest who analysed it in his 1561 chess book. It's also called the Spanish Opening.
famous: The main weapon of Fischer, Kasparov and nearly every world champion.
fact: In the 2000 World Championship, Kramnik used the Berlin Defence against it to neutralise Kasparov's attack — fans nicknamed it the "Berlin Wall".
memory: Bishop to b5 hits the knight that defends e5: attack the defender.
when: When you want rich middlegames with long-term pressure. Suits patient, strategic players.
ideas: Bb5 pressures the c6 knight, which guards e5.
Castle, play Re1, c3 and d4 to build a big centre.
The bishop retreats to a4 and b3, staying on the a2–g8 diagonal aiming at f7.
Nbd2–f1–g3 brings the knight to the kingside.
watch: Bxc6 then Nxe5 does NOT win a pawn early: Black gets it back with ...Qd4 or ...Qg5.
Watch for the Noah's Ark trap: ...b5 and ...c4 can trap your bishop on b3.

story: Named after an 1824 correspondence match between Edinburgh and London, where the Edinburgh team played it.

fact: Correspondence matches like Edinburgh–London took years, with moves sent by post.
memory: Scotch = straight to the point: d4 on move three.

name: Queen's Gambit
personality: Solid and strategic: offer a wing pawn to win the centre.
story: One of the oldest openings: it appears in a manuscript from Göttingen around 1490.
famous: A pillar of world-championship chess for over 100 years.
fact: The 2020 Netflix series "The Queen's Gambit" made chess boards sell out worldwide.
memory: It's a gambit in name only — if Black takes on c4, you usually win the pawn back.
when: When you want rich, strategic games and lasting pressure. Perfect with 1.d4.
ideas: c4 challenges Black's d5 pawn and fights for the centre.
Nc3, Bg5 and e3 develop smoothly.
If Black takes on c4, play e3/e4 and Bxc4 to regain it with a big centre.
Later, the minority attack (b4–b5) is a classic plan.

name: London System
personality: Same setup every game: Bf4, e3, c3, and a rock-solid pyramid.
story: It takes its name from the 1922 London tournament, where it was played several times.
famous: Modern top players like Magnus Carlsen have used it to dodge heavy theory.
fact: Club players love it because you can play it against almost any Black setup.
memory: Bishop out BEFORE e3 — otherwise it gets locked inside the pawn chain.
when: When you want a reliable system with little memorisation.
ideas: Get the dark-squared bishop to f4 before playing e3.
Build the pyramid: d4, e3, c3.
Knights to f3 and d2, bishop to d3, then castle.
Later, Ne5 and a kingside push (h4, g4) are typical attacking plans.
watch: Black's ...c5 and ...Qb6 attack b2 early — be ready with Qb3 or Qc2.
If Black plays ...Nh5, keep your bishop safe with Bg3 or Be5.

story: Named after the English champion Howard Staunton, who played it against Saint-Amant in their famous 1843 match.
famous: Botvinnik, Karpov and Kasparov all relied on it.
fact: It's like a Sicilian Defence with colours reversed — and an extra move for White.
memory: c4 grabs d5 from the flank; the bishop on g2 watches the long diagonal.
when: When you prefer manoeuvring games over sharp tactics.
ideas: Control d5 with c4, Nc3 and Bg2.
Fianchetto your bishop on g2 to rake the long diagonal.
Castle and expand on the queenside with a3, b4.
watch: Black can grab space with ...e5 and ...d5 — don't let them build a perfect centre for free.
If Black's knight lands on d4, think about exchanging it.

personality: Pure romance: sacrifice the f-pawn on move two and attack.
story: The darling of the 1800s romantic era, when brave sacrifices were the fashion.

fact: Anderssen gave up both rooks, a bishop and his queen in the Immortal Game — and still won.
memory: f4 = fight for f-file and the centre: trade your f-pawn for Black's e-pawn.
when: When you want wild attacking games and your opponent may not know the theory.
ideas: 2.f4 lures Black's e-pawn away from the centre.
Play d4 and Bxf4 to win the pawn back with a huge centre.
Castle and use the half-open f-file against f7.
watch: Beware ...Qh4+ early — your king can't castle and gets chased.
After 2...exf4 3.Nf3 d5! Black strikes back in the centre; don't panic.

story: Named after the Vienna chess players who studied it in the 1800s.

fact: It lets you play King's-Gambit-style attacks with less risk.
memory: Nc3 first guards e4, so f4 comes with extra force.

famous: Bobby Fischer and Garry Kasparov made it their main weapon.
fact: The Sicilian is the most popular reply to 1.e4 at master level.
memory: ...a6 is the Najdorf's signature: it keeps White's pieces off b5.

ideas: ...c5 fights for d4 from the side, creating an unbalanced game.

name: Nimzo-Indian Defence
personality: Pin the knight, fight for e4, and give White doubled pawns.
story: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, author of the famous book "My System" (1925).
famous: Considered one of Black's most respected defences; Capablanca, Botvinnik and Kasparov all played it.
fact: Nimzowitsch loved "prophylaxis" — stopping the opponent's plans before they start.
memory: ...Bb4 pins the knight that wants to support e4.
when: When you want a strategic fight with clear, sound ideas.
ideas: ...Bb4 pins Nc3 and fights for the e4 square.
Be ready to take on c3, giving White doubled pawns.
Strike with ...c5 and ...d5, or set up ...b6 and ...Bb7.
watch: If White gets the bishop pair and opens the position, those bishops can be strong.
Against 4.Qc2, White avoids doubled pawns — play ...O-O and ...d5 or ...c5.
moves: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 e3 O-O Bd3 d5 Nf3 c5 O-O

name: Grünfeld Defence
personality: Let White build a big centre, then blast it with pieces.
story: Introduced by Austrian grandmaster Ernst Grünfeld in 1922.
famous: Bobby Fischer's "Game of the Century" (1956, vs Donald Byrne) was a Grünfeld.
fact: Fischer was just 13 when he played the Game of the Century.
memory: ...d5, swap on c3, then hit d4 with ...Bg7, ...c5 and ...Nc6.
when: When you love dynamic, concrete positions and know your lines.
ideas: Trade knights so White's centre has fewer defenders.
Pressure d4 with the g7 bishop, ...c5 and ...Nc6.
If the centre cracks, your pieces become very active.
watch: White's big centre can roll forward (d5) if you're too slow.
This is a theory-heavy opening — drill the lines.
moves: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 cxd5 Nxd5 e4 Nxc3 bxc3 Bg7 Nf3 c5 Be3

name: Dutch Defence
personality: Grab e4 with ...f5 and aim for a kingside attack.
story: Named after Elias Stein, a Dutch-based player who recommended it in 1789.
famous: Botvinnik played it in world championship matches; Magnus Carlsen uses it now and then.
fact: It's the mirror image of the Sicilian idea — but with the f-pawn, near your own king.
memory: ...f5 controls e4; then ...Nf6, ...e6, ...Be7 and castle.
when: When you want unbalanced, attacking chances against 1.d4.
ideas: ...f5 fights for e4 and prepares kingside play.
Castle quickly — the f-pawn has moved, so king safety matters.
Typical plans: ...Qe8–h5 or ...d6 and ...e5.
watch: The e8–h5 diagonal is weak early: watch for checks like Qh5+.
The Staunton Gambit (2.e4) leads to sharp play — know it.

name: Counter: vs the London System
personality: Hit the London's weak spot — b2 — before White's setup is finished.
story: Because the London's bishop leaves c1 early, the b2 pawn loses a defender.
famous: This ...c5 + ...Qb6 plan is a standard antidote used at all levels.
fact: Many London players are caught out by quick pressure on b2.
memory: Bishop left c1? Queen to b6 hits b2.
when: Whenever your opponent plays d4 and an early Bf4.
ideas: ...c5 challenges d4 straight away.
...Qb6 attacks b2 — the London bishop no longer guards it.
After Qb3, ...c4 gains space and kicks the queen.
watch: Don't grab b2 if it traps your queen — check Nc3, Rb1 ideas first.
Keep developing; the London is solid once it's set up.
moves: d4 d5 Bf4 c5 e3 Nc6 c3 Qb6 Qb3 c4 Qc2 Nf6

name: Counter: vs the Scandinavian
personality: Gain time on Black's early queen and develop with tempo.
story: White's simple plan is to use the queen's early outing to develop faster.
famous: Nc3 with tempo is the most popular answer at every level.
fact: Every time you kick the queen, you gain a free developing move.
memory: Queen out early? Knight to c3 says hello.
when: When your opponent answers 1.e4 with 1...d5.
ideas: Take on d5, then Nc3 hits the queen.
Develop quickly: d4, Nf3, Bc4, castle.
Use your lead in development to open lines.
watch: Don't chase the queen pointlessly — develop while you do it.
Watch for ...Bg4 pinning your f3 knight.

name: Counter: vs the King's Gambit
personality: Take the pawn, then strike back in the centre with ...d5.
story: The Modern Defence (3...d5) gives the pawn back for quick, healthy development.
famous: A reliable choice used by many strong players.
fact: Returning the gambit pawn at the right moment kills a lot of White's attack.
memory: Take on f4, then ...d5 — fight fire with central fire.
when: Whenever someone throws the King's Gambit at you.
ideas: 2...exf4 accepts the gambit.
3...d5 opens lines for your pieces.
Develop with ...Nf6, ...Nxd5, ...Be7 and castle.
watch: Don't hang on to the extra pawn at all costs.
Watch your f7 square against Bc4 ideas.

name: Counter: vs the Englund Gambit
personality: Keep the extra pawn and dodge the famous queen trap.
story: The Englund Gambit (1...e5) is a trappy line seen a lot in fast online games.
famous: Named after Swedish player Fritz Englund.
fact: Its trap — 4.Bf4? Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Bc3?? Bb4! — catches many players.
memory: Against ...Qe7, guard b2 and don't let the queen land there with check.
when: When your opponent answers 1.d4 with 1...e5.
ideas: Take the pawn: 2.dxe5.
After ...Qe7, Qd5 attacks and holds e5.
Develop normally and stay a pawn up.
watch: 4.Bf4? Qb4+! hits b2 and the bishop.
Don't let Black's queen land on b2 with tempo.

name: Counter: vs the Stonewall Attack
personality: Develop your light bishop early and hit the centre with ...c5.
story: The Stonewall Attack (d4, e3, Bd3, f4) aims at your king with a pawn wall in the centre.
famous: Popular among club attackers.
fact: Its weak spot is the e4 square and White's locked-in c1 bishop.
memory: Get the c8 bishop out before ...e6, then ...c5.
when: When you see d4, e3, Bd3 and f4.
ideas: Play ...Bg4 or ...Bf5 before ...e6.
...c5 pressures d4.
A knight on e4 can be a great outpost.
watch: Watch for Ne5 followed by g4–g5 kingside attacks.
Don't castle into a ready-made attack without counterplay.
moves: d4 d5 e3 Nf6 Bd3 c5 c3 Nc6 f4 Bg4 Nf3 e6
